extracted.intended_audience: employers, employment counsel, policymakers, labor advocates, and commenters on the FTC non-compete rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards the Commission uses to evaluate non-compete clauses, especially those with senior executives, under Section 5 of the FTC Act and the final rule. Includes legal-elements tests, factual indicators (bargaining power, compensation, market effects), and policy considerations (existing contracts, alternatives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5 inquiry elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether conduct is an unfair method of competition under section 5, the Commission assesses two elements: (1) whether the conduct is a method of competition, as opposed to a condition of the marketplace; and (2) whether it is unfair, meaning that it goes beyond competition on the merits. The latter inquiry has two components: (a) whether the conduct has indicia of unfairness and (b) whether the conduct tends to negatively affect competitive conditions. These two components are weighed according to a sliding scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the primary legal framework used throughout the analysis: first classify the conduct as a 'method of competition' (not merely a market condition), then assess unfairness via indicia and tendency-to-harm. The Commission may weigh the two unfairness components on a sliding scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of competition vs condition of the marketplace
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes with senior executives are evaluated on whether they are a 'method of competition' rather than a condition of the marketplace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission finds non-competes with senior executives are a method of competition for the same reasons as non-competes with other workers (see Part IV.C.2.a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Facial indicia of unfairness: restrictive and exclusionary nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes are 'facially unfair conduct' because they are restrictive and exclusionary — they restrict competitive activity (preventing workers from seeking or accepting other work or starting a business) and impair rivals' opportunities (impair a rival firm's ability to hire or a new entrant's ability to form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the non-compete's nature and function restrict competition and exclude rivals, with special attention to senior executives' scarcity and specialized skills that make exclusion particularly harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to negatively affect competitive conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry asks whether the conduct tends to negatively affect competitive conditions in product and service markets and in labor markets; direct proof of specific-instance harm is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission evaluates tendency using empirical literature, comment record, theory (e.g., matching frictions, buyout inefficiencies), and aggregate effects; no separate market-definition or showing of market power is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on new business formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes with senior executives tend to inhibit new business formation by blocking executives from forming new businesses and by preventing startups from assembling necessary leadership teams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence considered includes executive strategic expertise, role in forming leadership teams, empirical studies showing top management hires increase startup growth/success. Consider both individual and prevalence effects (aggregate prevalence can inhibit formation even if individual use varies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes with senior executives tend to inhibit innovation by impeding efficient matching between executives and firms and reducing knowledge flow and cross-pollination of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether non-competes prevent firms from hiring executives who maximize innovation capacity, whether executives' external networks and mobility (shorter tenures, external hires) correlate with greater innovation, and whether aggregate prevalence reduces overall innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on labor markets: suppression of mobility and earnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes reduce labor mobility and worker earnings for senior executives in the same way they do for other workers—by directly restricting seeking/accepting work or starting a business after employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider empirical evidence of mobility/earnings suppression and whether senior-executive non-competes produce similar or greater labor-market harms given executives' roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploitative or coercive analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether non-competes are 'exploitative or coercive' (especially at contracting or departure) depends on bargaining power indicators: whether the worker negotiated terms, had counsel, received meaningful consideration (higher wages, severance), or faced threats/pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission found senior executives are 'substantially less likely' to be exploited or coerced based on bargaining indicators, but does not categorically rule out exploitation; examine evidence such as negotiation with counsel, severance length relative to non-compete, and reports of one-sided/required non-competes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bargaining power not conferred by title alone; consider earnings/job duties
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere job title alone is insufficient to infer bargaining power; lower-earning senior executives can be subject to the same exploitation and coercion as other workers. The final rule uses both an earnings test and a job duties test to identify 'senior executive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess actual bargaining power with attention to income and duties rather than relying solely on the label 'senior executive.' The rule's operational definition (see next metric) captures workers more likely to have complex compensation and bargaining leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'senior executive' (earnings + job duties test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule defines 'senior executive' to refer to workers earning more than $151,164 who are in a 'policy-making position' as defined in the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definitional rule is used to determine which existing non-competes may remain in force; it captures workers likely to have complex compensation and greater bargaining power. Evaluate eligibility against both the earnings threshold and the policy-making duties test.

rubrics_metrics.name: In terrorem effects and prohibiting threats/misrepresentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers' misrepresentations that a worker is subject to a non-compete (or is enforceable) and threats to litigate can have in terrorem effects that deter workers from seeking work, even if the non-compete is unenforceable; the final rule therefore prohibits threatening to enforce or representing applicability where the rule renders such non-competes unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether employers represented non-competes as valid (even without good-faith basis) or threatened litigation; such conduct is prohibited because it tends to deter competition irrespective of legal enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical impacts of extinguishing existing non-competes for senior executives
rubrics_metrics.description: Even while finding senior-executive non-competes unfair methods of competition, the Commission allows existing non-competes with senior executives to remain in force due to practical impacts of extinguishing them (complex compensation packages, potential disruption).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy balances competitive harms with practical consequences of retroactive extinguishment; consider transitional fairness and administrative/practical burdens when deciding treatment of existing agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buyout clauses and buyout-prohibition as inadequate remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibiting buyout clauses or relying on buyouts is not an adequate alternative to banning non-competes: buyouts can make it harder for executives to escape non-competes (fewer executives could escape), create inefficiently high payments, and not address tendency to reduce mobility and efficient matching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate arguments that buyouts preserve efficiency; the Commission rejects buyout-only remedies based on theoretical and empirical analysis (e.g., Shi) showing buyouts create deadweight loss and may worsen mobility/matching problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of less restrictive alternatives to protect investments
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing competitive effects, consider whether employers have less restrictive alternatives (other than non-competes) to protect firm investments such as trade secrets, and whether such alternatives are available for senior executives as well as other workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If viable, less-restrictive alternatives exist, that undercuts the necessity defense for non-competes; the Commission finds employers generally have less-restrictive options and that these weigh against permitting non-competes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality-of-record evidentiary standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission's findings rest on the totality of the record: review of the empirical literature, the public comment record, and the Commission's expertise in identifying practices that impair competitive conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions are supported by combining empirical studies, widespread comment evidence (including worker anecdotes), and economic/legal analysis rather than relying on any single type of evidence.
